name: Wisdom tooth removal

lead: Wisdom teeth, the third molars, usually erupt between about 17 and 21. When they lack room they can become impacted, and they are commonly removed to treat or prevent decay, gum infection or pain. Some looksmaxxers also discuss removal as a way to protect front-tooth alignment or relate it to jaw development.

Some clinicians have removed them to prevent crowding, which is disputed: research has found no agreed view that wisdom teeth cause lower incisor crowding, and the jaw-shape link is forum theory. NICE guidance (2000) and the American Public Health Association oppose prophylactic removal, and a 2020 Cochrane review found evidence insufficient to settle the question.

paras: Removal is an oral surgery procedure, often with a flap and bone removal for impacted teeth. Swelling and pain after surgery are the common effects studied in trials of drugs and techniques, and people typically plan recovery time.
Removing lower third molars can damage the inferior alveolar nerve temporarily or permanently, reported in about 1 in 85 patients. Other risks include dry socket, swelling and infection.

angle.text: Wisdom teeth are routinely removed when impacted, and some looksmaxxers also discuss removal as a way to protect front-tooth alignment or relate it to jaw development. The crowding link is disputed among clinicians, and the jaw-shape link is based on forum theory.

lead: Wisdom tooth removal is the extraction of the third molars, the last teeth to come in, which typically erupt between about 17 and 21.[1] People in looksmaxxing and dental circles discuss it in terms of smile and bite: when a wisdom tooth is impacted or crowded against the second molar, taking it out can relieve pain, infection and decay in the back of the mouth, and some patients and clinicians have also hoped that removal protects the alignment of the front teeth.[1]

Wisdom teeth are the most commonly impacted teeth, and impaction can lead to decay, gum disease and pericoronitis (inflammation of the gum around a partly erupted tooth).[1] The UK health service describes extraction as usually done under local anaesthetic, taking a few minutes up to about 40, with most people home the same day and full recovery in up to about two weeks.[2] Swelling, bruising on the cheek and a stiff jaw are described as common in the first days.[2]

Whether healthy, symptom-free wisdom teeth should be removed in advance is a long-running professional debate. The UK's NICE guidance (2000) opposes prophylactic removal, the American Public Health Association took a similar position, and a 2020 Cochrane review (Ghaeminia and colleagues) judged the evidence very low quality and unable to settle the question.[1][3] The idea that wisdom teeth push the lower front teeth into crowding is also disputed; Wikipedia's summaries state that eruption of wisdom teeth is not believed to cause front-tooth crowding, and a UK randomised trial found insufficient evidence to justify removal solely to prevent incisor crowding.[1][3][1]

In looksmaxxing forums the topic connects to jaw-development ideas: members who pursue palate or midface expansion, forward-growth devices or tongue posture ask whether upper or lower wisdom teeth should be kept or removed, while patients heading for orthognathic (jaw) surgery meet the question in a surgical context.[4][5] Dental sources frame the decision around pathology, position and age rather than appearance.[2][3]

paras: Wisdom teeth develop between about ages 14 and 25: half of root formation is complete by 16 and about 95 percent of teeth have erupted by 25, although some movement continues later.[3] Most erupt between 17 and 21, eruption tends to occur earlier in people of African heritage than in people of Asian or European heritage, and a tooth that has not erupted by 25 is generally considered unlikely to do so by itself.[1] Missing third molars occur in 9 to 30 percent of studied populations, with wide variation between groups linked to genes such as PAX9 and MSX1.[3][1]

Anthropologists propose that primate wisdom teeth helped chew tough foods, and that the shift to agriculture more than 10,000 years ago, and later the Industrial Revolution, brought softer diets associated with shorter, wider mandibles and higher risk of crowding and malocclusion.[1] Wikipedia notes that impaction became roughly ten times more common in the industrial era, that the oldest known impacted wisdom tooth belongs to a European woman who lived around 13,000 to 11,000 BCE, and that the Latin name dentes sapientiae descends from a Hippocratic term.[3][1] Wikipedia presents the diet and jaw-size accounts as suggestions that are not firmly established.[3]

Teeth are described as developing, erupted, embedded or impacted; impacted teeth fail to erupt because another tooth blocks them. Lower third molars are commonly classified by direction (mesioangular, tilted forward, is most common), depth and the Pell and Gregory system, and age is described as the most reliable predictor of extraction difficulty and complications, more so than orientation.[3]

Impaction occurs when the jaws lack room for all the teeth, with a genetic contribution to jaw and tooth size.[3] A New Zealand study found 95.6 percent of young adults had at least one wisdom tooth, and a Swedish study reported impacted lower third molars in 72 percent of participants.[3] Pericoronitis, infection of the gum over a partly erupted tooth, is the most common pathology after age 20.[3]

Extraction treats or prevents decay, pericoronitis, gum disease and cysts associated with impacted teeth. Pathology occurs in about 12% of impacted cases, with cysts in roughly 0.64% to 2.24%.[1] Studies cited in the encyclopedia literature suggest that 30% to 60% of people with symptom-free impacted teeth end up needing at least one extracted within 4 to 12 years.[1]

The NHS lists reasons for removal as lack of room to emerge fully, partial coverage by gum, pain, swelling, food trapping, decay, cysts and abscesses, and says teeth causing no problems are usually left in place and monitored.[2] A review on the asymptomatic, disease-free wisdom tooth frames the decision as one of removal versus retention.[6]

In the 1970s unerupted wisdom teeth were thought to push the lower front teeth together. Crowding has several causes, including tooth size, skeletal growth, age and sex, and wisdom teeth alone do not appear to cause it.[1] This is why orthodontic crowding is a commonly cited but disputed reason for prophylactic removal.[1]

Many impacted teeth are extracted before age 25, before symptoms appear, which created the controversy over removing disease-free teeth.[3] NICE stopped routine NHS removal of asymptomatic, disease-free third molars in 2000, citing no reliable evidence of benefit and the risks and costs of surgery; operations fell between 2000 and 2006 and the average age at extraction rose from 25 to 31.[3]

Critics of that policy note that wisdom teeth can cause decay or gum disease on the adjacent second molar and that monitoring has costs; Wikipedia reports lower second-molar decay in the UK rising from 4 to 5 percent to 19 percent after NICE, and a 2014 study finding UK hospitalisations for impacted teeth about five times lower than in France.[3] The 2020 Cochrane review found removal may be associated with a higher long-term risk of gum disease on the second molar, but with very low-quality evidence, and no clear evidence on crowding or decay; it noted that early removal before 25, good hygiene and no prior periodontal disease improve outcomes.[3] Studies cited by Wikipedia find that 30 to 60 percent of people with symptom-free impacted teeth have at least one extracted within 4 to 12 years.[3][1] A 2024 survey reported by Wikipedia found 53 percent of Americans had had wisdom teeth removed, versus 26 percent of those aged 18 to 29.[1]

sections.h: Relation to jaw surgery and facial change
paras: Wisdom tooth removal and orthognathic surgery intersect. Wikipedia's orthognathic surgery article describes a study by Lacy and Colcleugh of 83 patients (1987 to 1991) in which patients who had third molars removed at the same time as a mandibular sagittal split osteotomy developed hardware infection in 73 percent of cases, and it concludes that doing both together raises infection risk; before 1991 some patients had both done together.[5]

Orthognathic surgery usually produces a noticeable change in facial appearance, and its article describes planning with software that predicts the post-surgery face.[5] Wisdom tooth removal alone is a dental procedure: no trials were identified that measure facial appearance after it, although facial swelling for a few days is common and is the most-studied short-term effect.[7][8]

The gum is opened if it covers the tooth, bone around the tooth may be widened, and the tooth is lifted out whole or in sections, with dissolvable stitches if needed.[2] Surgeons have compared techniques such as piezosurgery with conventional rotating instruments in split-mouth trials, and have compared panoramic radiography with cone-beam CT for planning moderate-risk lower impactions.[9][10]

Facial swelling is a prominent short-term effect. A review of strategies to limit postoperative swelling after lower third molar surgery covers corticosteroids, antibiotics and other approaches, and a randomised split-mouth trial found that perioperative dexamethasone reduced post-surgical sequelae.[7][11] A Cochrane review examined ibuprofen and paracetamol for pain relief after lower wisdom tooth surgery.[12]

Removing lower third molars can damage the inferior alveolar nerve in about 1 in 85 patients (about 1 in 300 extractions), with higher risk for deeper impactions and roots close to the mandibular canal.[1] The NHS lists dry socket, infection and temporary or longer-lasting numbness or tingling of the tongue, lip or chin as risks.[2] A review of 339 third molar removals analysed complications after surgery.[13]

sections.h: Recovery and aftercare as described by health services
paras: The NHS states most people return to normal activities the next day, with harder extractions or general anaesthesia needing 1 to 3 days off work, and pain and swelling for up to two weeks that usually begin improving after one or two days, with cheek bruising and a stiff jaw possible.[2] It lists dry socket, infection and nerve damage causing numbness or tingling in the tongue, lips or chin as risks, notes nerve symptoms usually improve but can last weeks or months, and advises contacting a dentist or NHS 111 for bleeding that will not stop, severe or worsening pain, bad taste or fever.[2]

Wikipedia reports that in a 2005 survey of 535 California oral surgeons the rate of inferior alveolar nerve injury was about 1 in 2,500, while published rates range from 0.04 to 5 percent, a variation attributed to technique, patient population and surgeon experience; another figure often cited is about 1 in 85 patients.[3][1] Coronectomy, removal of the crown while leaving the roots, reduces nerve risk but can lead to root migration or reoperation.[3] A Cochrane review found antibiotics before or after surgery reduced infection, pain and dry socket but caused more side effects, with about 19 patients needing antibiotics to prevent one infection.[3] Bone loss next to the second molar was reported in 43 percent of patients aged 25 or older.[3]

Many randomised trials have studied postoperative outcomes. A split-mouth trial of dexamethasone reported reduced sequelae after lower third molar surgery,[7] a Cochrane review examined ibuprofen and paracetamol for pain relief,[12] a split-mouth trial compared piezosurgery with the traditional technique,[9] and a randomised trial compared panoramic radiography with cone-beam CT for predicting outcomes.[10] A review of removal versus retention addresses disease-free teeth.[6] A trial of manual lymph drainage after impacted third molar removal examined postoperative facial swelling and discomfort.[8]
These studies address recovery and complications. No trials were identified that measure facial appearance after wisdom tooth removal.

A looksmax.org thread asks whether to cancel removal and try midface expansion (MSE) instead, citing upper wisdom teeth stuck behind the second molars; the poster says expansion could make space for the teeth, widen the smile and help nasal airways. Replies discuss expansion, pulling teeth forward and keeping the lower wisdom teeth if they are erupting straight.[4] Dental guidance bases removal decisions on clinical assessment of pathology and position.[1][2]
